entry.title: Chasing a moving optimum: the mistake no Bayesian optimizer can avoid

link.title: Chasing a moving optimum: the mistake no Bayesian optimizer can avoid

entry.content:
Many systems must keep learning after they are deployed, because the world they operate in keeps changing. A recommender system faces shifting tastes, the best gains of a controller drift as its hardware wears out, and an LLM in production meets new topics, new users and new usage patterns, so that the prompt or the decoding settings that work best today may not work best next month. Such systems must keep adapting from feedback while they are in use: this is continual learning. Can they eventually stop making mistakes?

Let us study this question under the setting of time-varying Bayesian optimization and try to come up with an exact answer. A Bayesian optimizer searches for the maximum of an expensive black-box function \(f\), one noisy evaluation at a time: for instance, the performance of a deployed system as a function of its configuration \(x\) (the gains of the controller, the decoding settings of the LLM), measured through noisy feedback. It models \(f\) with a Gaussian process and queries the input \(x\) where \(f\) could plausibly be highest. In the vanilla, static case where \(f\) does not change, the uncertainty of the model about the location of the maximum vanishes as observations accumulate, and the optimizer eventually stops making mistakes. If \(f\) changes over time, the maximum at a given time \(t\), \(x^*_t = \arg\max_{x} f(x, t)\) moves, and this becomes a tracking problem where old observations lose relevance.

Let us make things more precise before going forward.

The model

Time-varying Bayesian optimization models the objective as a Gaussian process \(f(x, t)\) with zero mean, where \(x \in [0, 1]^d\) is the input and \(t\) is time. Its kernel is a product,

\[k ig((x, t), (x', t') ig) = k_S(x, x')\, k_T(t - t'),\]

where the spatial kernel \(k_S\) says how correlated the values of \(f\) at two inputs \(x\) and \(x'\) are, and the temporal kernel \(k_T\) how correlated they are at two times \(t\) and \(t'\). Both equal 1 at zero distance. The optimizer observes \(f\) every \(\Delta\) units of time: at time \(t_i = i\Delta\), it queries an input \(x_i\) and observes \(y_i = f(x_i, t_i) + \varepsilon_i\), where \(\varepsilon_i\) is Gaussian noise with variance \(\sigma_0^2\). Its mistake at step \(i\) is the regret

\[r_i = \max_x f(x, t_i) - f(x_i, t_i),\]

the gap between the value of the best input at time \(t_i\) and the value of the query. An algorithm is no-regret if its average regret \(R_n / n = rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n r_i\) goes to zero.

Four classes of temporal kernels

Let us recall the very useful Bochner’s theorem, stating that a stationary kernel is a superposition of oscillations:

\[k_T(t) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} S_T(\omega)\, e^{2\pi i \omega t}\, d\omega,\]

where \(S_T(\omega) \geq 0\) is the share of the variance at frequency \(\omega\), in cycles per unit of time, and is called the spectral density of \(k_T\). \(S_T\) has two possible components: a continuous part, which spreads variance over intervals of frequencies, and Dirac deltas, which put a finite share of the variance on single frequencies. The temporal kernels used in practice fall into four classes:

Class Spectral density Examples
Broadband continuous, positive at all frequencies RBF, Matérn
Band-limited continuous, zero outside a band \([- au, au]\) sinc, sinc²
Almost periodic infinitely many Dirac deltas periodic
Low-rank finitely many Dirac deltas sum of cosines, constant

In the following, it will be useful to distinguish a temporal kernel with no continuous part in its spectral density \(S_T\), i.e., if it is almost periodic or low-rank. I will call them rhythmic. For rythmic kernels, \(k_T(t) = \alpha_0 + 2\sum_{p \geq 1} \alpha_p \cos(2\pi\omega_p t)\) with weights \(\alpha_p \geq 0\): the objective is a superposition of oscillations at fixed frequencies, such as daily and weekly cycles. A static objective, with \(k_T \equiv 1\), is the simplest rhythmic case: a single Dirac delta at \(\omega = 0\).

Below, you can find a visualization of spectral densities of the four kernel classes and an example of function drawn from the resulting Gaussian process. Feel free to play with it and make yourself familiar with these classes.

How well does the past predict the present?

Fix an input \(x\). Since \(k_S(x, x) = 1\), the values \((f(x, t))_t\) form a Gaussian process in time with kernel \(k_T\). Suppose that a noisy version \(y_i\) of \(f\) is observed at \(x\) at every step \(t_i\), and let \(e_n = \mathrm{Var}[f(x, t_n) \mid y_0, \cdots, y_{n-1}]\) be the variance of the present value \(f(x, t_n)\) given the \(n\) previous noisy observations. For a static objective, \(e_n = \sigma_0^2 / (n + \sigma_0^2)\), which goes to zero. Below, three temporal kernels are compared, with \(\sigma_0^2 = 0.01\): a constant kernel, a periodic kernel and an RBF kernel. The last two change at the same speed: the correlation between consecutive values, \(k_T(\Delta)\), is 0.988 for both.

For the constant kernel, \(e_n\) decreases like \(1/n\), as predicted. For the periodic kernel, \(e_n\) stays close to that of the RBF kernel during the first period (40 steps), then also decreases like \(1/n\). For the RBF kernel, \(e_n\) stops decreasing after about 30 steps, at \(0.016\): no amount of past observations appears to lower this variance. If we want to understand the asymptotic performance of a Bayesian optimizer in a time-varying setting, a quantity that seems interesting to study is \(e_\infty = \lim_{n o \infty} e_n\), the uncertainty of the model about the present given an infinite past.

The information rate

The \(n\)-th observation \(y_n\) is informative only if there is still some uncertainty about \(f(x, t_n)\) given the previous observations \(\{y_1, \cdots, y_{n-1}\}\), and we have seen that this uncertainty is given by \(e_{n-1}\). To quantify the information that \(y_n\) brings about \(f(x, \cdot)\), in nats, we can use Shannon’s formula for a Gaussian channel:

\[I_n = rac{1}{2}\log\left(1 + rac{e_{n-1}}{\sigma_0^2} ight).\]

Taking the limit, we get the information rate \( ho = \lim_{n o \infty} I_n\), the information that each new observation brings given an infinite past. Solving for \(e_\infty\):

\[e_\infty = \sigma_0^2\left(e^{2 ho} - 1 ight).\]

Hence, a model will face an irreducible uncertainty (\(e_\infty > 0\)), even when having access to infinitely many past observations, if and only if each observation keeps bringing new information (\( ho > 0\)). For the RBF kernel above, \( ho \approx 0.48\) nats per observation; for the constant and periodic kernels, \( ho = 0\).

The information rate can actually be computed from the spectral density \(S_T\). Sampling every \(\Delta\) units of time folds all frequencies onto \([0, 1/2]\) cycle per observation (aliasing). Let \(s_\Delta( u)\) be the continuous part of the folded spectral density at frequency \( u\). Then1

\[ ho = \int_0^{1/2} \log\left(1 + rac{s_\Delta( u)}{\sigma_0^2} ight) d u.\]

This is Shannon’s formula applied frequency by frequency, with signal-to-noise ratio \(s_\Delta( u) / \sigma_0^2\). On a logarithmic scale, \( ho\) is the area between the spectrum \(s_\Delta + \sigma_0^2\) and the noise level \(\sigma_0^2\). Dirac deltas do not enter the formula: they have zero width, hence zero area.

Here is a visualization of the equation above. Play with the noise level to see how it impacts the informative rate \( ho\) and the irreducible uncertainty \(e_\infty\). For rhythmic kernels, you are given the opportunity to build a mixture with a broadband kernel (RBF).

Two consequences follow. A rhythmic kernel has \( ho = 0\) and \(e_\infty = 0\). A kernel with a continuous part, even one of tiny weight, has \( ho > 0\) and \(e_\infty > 0\), for every finite observation frequency \(1/\Delta\) and every observational noise \(\sigma_0^2 > 0\). In short: even with an infinite past, the uncertainty about the present vanishes if and only if the temporal kernel is rhythmic.

Rhythms are learned once and for all

Why do rhythms bring no information in the long run? Using \(\cos(2\pi\omega(t - t')) = \cos(2\pi\omega t)\cos(2\pi\omega t') + \sin(2\pi\omega t)\sin(2\pi\omega t')\), an objective with a rhythmic temporal kernel can be written as

\[f(x, t) = \sum_{m} \sqrt{w_m}\,\psi_m(t)\,g_m(x),\]

where the \(\psi_m\) are known functions of time (a constant, and the cosine and sine of each frequency \(\omega_p\)), the \(w_m\) are the weights of the Dirac deltas in \(S_T\), and the \(g_m\) are independent static functions drawn from \(\mathcal{GP}(0, k_S)\). All the randomness is in the \(g_m\), drawn only once at the start. Predicting the objective at any future time only requires learning the \(g_m\), which is a static problem, as you can see below.

As observations accumulate, the posterior of every \(g_m\) concentrates, and so does the posterior of the objective at every future time. A continuous part admits no such decomposition into countably many static functions: new randomness enters at every instant, which makes the optimization problem inherently not static.

Band-limited objectives, the Nyquist rate and the noise

Band-limited kernels show that the observation noise is essential. A band-limited objective has no variation at frequencies above its cutoff \( au\). If it is observed faster than the Nyquist rate, \(1/\Delta > 2 au\), the folded spectrum \(s_\Delta\) is zero on part of \([0, 1/2]\). Without noise, such an objective can be predicted perfectly from a long enough past: the prediction variance goes to zero, even though the spectral density has a continuous part.2 With noise, it cannot: \(\log(1 + s_\Delta/\sigma_0^2)\) is positive wherever \(s_\Delta\) is, so \( ho > 0\) and \(e_\infty > 0\) for every \(\sigma_0^2 > 0\).

Below the Nyquist rate, aliasing folds the band onto itself, \(s_\Delta\) is positive everywhere, and \(e_\infty > 0\) even without noise. Observing \(k\) times faster, for an integer \(k\), can only reduce \(e_\infty\), but with noise it never makes it zero.

At \(\Delta = 5\) (twice the Nyquist rate), the noiseless prediction variance falls below \(10^{-6}\) within 20 observations and keeps decreasing to zero, while with noise variance \(0.01\) it stops at \(e_\infty \approx 0.11\). Decreasing the noise lowers \(e_\infty\) (to about \(10^{-4}\) for a noise variance of \(10^{-8}\)) but never cancels it. Beyond \(\Delta = 10\), the two curves stop at almost the same level: aliasing, not noise, limits the prediction.

From irreducible uncertainty to an unavoidable mistake

An optimizer does not observe \(f(x, t_i)\), with a fixed \(x\) at every step \(i\). It moves, and through \(k_S\), an observation at one input informs the others. However, this does not beat the constraint imposed by \(e_\infty\). An observation at \(x_i\) is a noisy measurement of \(k_S(x_i, x)\, f(x, t_i)\) plus a term independent of \(f(x, \cdot)\). Because \(k_S\) can be seen as a correlation function without loss of generality (\(\lvert k_S(x_i, x) vert \leq 1\) w.l.o.g.), it is less informative about \(f(x, \cdot)\) than an observation at \(x\) itself. Hence, for every algorithm and every input \(x\),

\[\mathrm{Var}\left[f(x, t_n) \mid y_1, \dots, y_{n-1} ight] \geq e_{n-1} \geq e_\infty.\]

The same argument applies to the difference between the values at the query \(x_n\) and at an input \(x'\) far from it: its posterior variance stays above \(2c_S\, e_\infty\), where \(c_S > 0\) is a positive constant that depends only on \(k_S\). The optimizer can therefore never be absolutely sure that \(x_n\) is better than \(x'\). With a probability strictly greater than zero, we can show it is not, and the instantaneous regret \(r_n \geq f(x', t_n) - f(x_n, t_n)\) is positive.

To summarize, we have two complementary results.

Theorem 1. If the spectral density of \(k_T\) has a continuous part, there is a constant \(c > 0\), which depends only on \(k_S\), \(k_T\), \(\Delta\) and \(\sigma_0^2\), such that for every algorithm (deterministic or randomized) and every step \(n\), \(\mathbb{E}[r_n] \geq c\). Hence \(\mathbb{E}[R_n] \in \Theta(n)\), and \(R_n \geq cn/2\) with a probability bounded away from zero.3

Theorem 2. If \(k_T\) is rhythmic, GP-UCB is no-regret under mild conditions. For a sum of \(L\) cosines and an RBF spatial kernel in \(d\) dimensions, \(R_n \in \mathcal{O} ig(\sqrt{(2L+1)\, n\, (\log n)^{d+2}} ig)\) with high probability: this is the rate of GP-UCB on a static objective, up to the factor \(2L + 1\).

The race below runs GP-UCB on two objectives that change at the same speed, as in the second figure: one with the periodic temporal kernel, one with the RBF temporal kernel.

On the RBF objective, the posterior variance at the present stays above \(e_\infty\) at every input, and the average regret stops decreasing. On the periodic objective, both keep decreasing.

These results also explain why previous regret bounds for time-varying Bayesian optimization are linear. Such bounds are expressed with the maximum information gain \(\gamma_n\), the largest information that \(n\) observations can bring about \(f\). Observing a single input at every step already brings at least \( ho\) nats per observation, so \(\gamma_n \geq ho n\), and every bound in terms of \(\gamma_n\) is linear when \( ho > 0\).

How large is the mistake?

Theorem 1 guarantees that the mistake does not vanish, but its magnitude could still be very small. What controls the size of the mistake in practice? To answer independently of any particular algorithm, consider an oracle that observes the whole objective on a grid of 100 inputs at every past step, with the same noise, and queries the maximizer of its posterior mean. No algorithm that queries one grid input per step can have a smaller expected regret.

Across the 15 kernels and three families, the regret of the oracle is approximately proportional to \(e_\infty\), over two orders of magnitude (log-log slope 1.07). The irreducible uncertainty seems to measure the intrinsic difficulty of the problem: a kernel with ten times the \(e_\infty\) costs about ten times the regret, whatever its family. GP-UCB, which observes one input per step, makes larger mistakes, as expected, and its regret grows more slowly with \(e_\infty\) (slope 0.46), but it ranks the kernels in the same order (Spearman correlation 0.95). Whether the proportionality holds exactly is an open question (and maybe the subject of a future note…)

What this means for continual learning

From no-regret to ε-optimality. When the world keeps producing information that its past cannot predict, asymptotic optimality, i.e., an average regret that goes to zero, is out of reach for every algorithm. A better goal is ε-optimality: an average regret that stays below a tolerance \(\varepsilon\) in the long run, \(\limsup_{n o \infty} \mathbb{E}[R_n] / n \leq \varepsilon\). The results above say which tolerances are within reach. Theorem 1 rules out every \(\varepsilon < c\), and the oracle shows that no algorithm querying one grid input per step goes below a level approximately proportional to \(e_\infty\). Algorithms can then be compared by how close their long-run regret comes to this level, rather than by whether they are no-regret. GP-UCB, for instance, stays up to 200 times above it on slowly changing objectives, so surely there is room for better algorithms!

A lower bound for harder problems. The setting of this note is favorable to the learner: the changes are stationary and Gaussian, their statistics are known exactly, and feedback arrives at a fixed rate. Real continual learning, for instance with a deployed LLM, cannot enjoy these simplifications. The theorems do not apply to such tasks directly. However, observe that the insight behind Theorem 1 concerns the world, not the learner: no learner, however large, can predict what its past does not determine. Whenever a task keeps producing information that its past cannot predict, its error has a positive floor, and having to learn the dynamics instead of knowing them can only increase the error. In this sense, the results are a lower bound for continual learning: they show that the floor exists and what lowers it, but not how high it is for a given task.

What lowers the floor. More past data and more computation do not lower it. More frequent or less noisy feedback does, without ever cancelling it. What recurs, such as daily or weekly cycles, can be learned once and for all. A continual learner should therefore separate what recurs, which it can learn, from what drifts, which it can only track with a positive error.

What decides between an error that vanishes and one that does not is not how fast the world changes with respect to the observation frequency, but whether it keeps producing information that its past cannot predict.

This note is based on joint work with Patrick Thiran. For more technical details, see our paper on arXiv.

  1. This is Pinsker’s formula for the mutual information rate between a stationary Gaussian sequence and its noisy observations. The folded density is \(s_\Delta( u) = rac{1}{\Delta}\sum_{\ell \in \mathbb{Z}} S_T^c ig(( u + \ell)/\Delta ig)\), where \(S_T^c\) is the continuous part of \(S_T\). The relation \(e_\infty = \sigma_0^2(e^{2 ho} - 1)\) is the Kolmogorov–Szegő formula applied to the noisy observations. ↩

  2. Without noise, the limit of the prediction variance is \(\exp ig(2\int_0^{1/2} \log s_\Delta( u)\, d u ig)\), which is zero when \(s_\Delta\) vanishes on an interval. It is reached only in the limit: for every finite \(n\), the prediction variance is positive. ↩

  3. Assumptions: a product kernel, a spatial kernel smooth enough for \(f\) to be Lipschitz in \(x\) with high probability, Gaussian noise, and observations at a fixed frequency. ↩
entry.summary: When the optimum of a time-varying problem keeps moving, can a Bayesian optimizer eventually stop making mistakes? Only if the changes can be predicted from the past; otherwise, every optimizer makes a mistake at every step, of a size set by the problem. Any system that must keep learning after deployment, from a controller to an LLM, faces the same limit.

entry.title: Symmetries as an inductive bias for a Bayesian optimizer

link.title: Symmetries as an inductive bias for a Bayesian optimizer

entry.content:
Some functions are invariant according to some symmetries. The energy of a molecule does not change when you rotate it, and a mixture of three powders is the same whatever order you list them in. When a function is unchanged by a group of transformations, a single evaluation tells you its value at several places at once. When evaluations are expensive, that is a powerful way to increase sample efficiency.

Take a wireless network. Below, two identical antennas serve sixteen people working along a corridor, and the goal is to place them so as to maximize the total throughput. A design of the wireless network is a pair of numbers, \(x = (x_1, x_2)\): the position of antenna 1 and the position of antenna 2. But the ordering of the antennas is arbitrary. Change it and you get another design, \((x_2, x_1)\), which describes the very same network.

Every network appears twice in the search space, once on each side of the diagonal, and the landscape is a mirror image of itself. That is worth exploiting. And the more antennas, the more worth it is: with \(n\) antennas, each network has \(n!\) labelings, and an optimizer that does not know it may pay for the same network up to \(n!\) times.

Now, the easiest way to grasp how useful symmetries could be is to play the optimizer yourself. Below is a hidden landscape with a few mirror symmetries. You have six evaluations to find its highest point. Then switch the symmetry on and play again.

This note is about incorporating these symmetries as an inductive bias for a Bayesian algorithm. It is based on our ICLR 2026 paper with Antoine Gonon, Aryan Ahadinia and Patrick Thiran, in which we revisit a simple idea from kernel methods, and show that it makes Bayesian optimization significantly more sample-efficient on symmetric problems.

Paying twice for the same information

Bayesian optimization looks for the maximum of a function that is expensive to evaluate and that offers no gradients: all you can do is query it and observe a (noisy) value. It maintains a probabilistic model of the function, usually a Gaussian process. After each evaluation, the model provides two things at every point \(x\): a best guess \(\mu(x)\), the posterior mean, and an uncertainty \(\sigma(x)\). The next query goes where the function could plausibly be highest,

\[x_{t+1} = \arg\max_x \; \mu_t(x) + \beta\,\sigma_t(x),\]

where a large \(\beta\) favors exploring uncertain regions and a small one favors refining the best region found so far. Everything the model believes comes from a single object, its kernel \(k(x, x') = \mathrm{Cov}(f(x), f(x'))\), which quantifies how similar the values of the function at \(x\) and \(x'\) should be. Here, as in the rest of this note, it is the Gaussian kernel \(k(x,x') = \exp\left(-\lVert x - x' \rVert^2 / 2\ell^2\right)\): nearby points are similar, distant ones are not.

The function below is symmetric: for any \(x\), \(f(x) = f(-x)\), but the model does not know it. Let the algorithm choose a few points and watch where it goes. Then tell the model about the mirror.

The symmetry-blind model sees an unexplored half and pays to evaluate it again, point by point. Once it knows the mirror, its uncertainty collapses on both sides at once and every evaluation lands somewhere new. With a single mirror, ignoring the symmetry roughly doubles the work. In real-world problems, a point can have thousands of copies.

Two ways to make a kernel invariant

Suppose that \(f\) is invariant under a group \(G\) of transformations: \(f(gx) = f(x)\) for every \(g \in G\) and every \(x\). Then \(x\) and \(gx\) are not merely similar, they are interchangeable. A Gaussian process whose sample paths all share this invariance must have an invariant kernel, with \(k(gx, g'x') = k(x, x')\) for all \(g, g' \in G\).1 Starting from a base kernel \(k\), there are two natural ways to build one:

\[k_{\mathrm{avg}}(x,x') = \frac{1}{\lvert G \rvert^2}\sum_{g,g'\in G} k(gx, g'x'), \qquad k_{\max}(x,x') = \max_{g,g'\in G}\, k(gx, g'x').\]

Both compare the copies of \(x\) with the copies of \(x'\). The first averages these similarities. It is the standard choice for Bayesian optimization, with a clean interpretation: the functions it can represent are exactly the invariant functions of the base kernel.2 The second keeps only the best alignment. Below, a group with \(n\) mirror lines gives \(x'\) its \(2n\) copies, and each segment links \(x\) to one of them, darker when they are more similar.

One thing becomes immediately clear: only one copy is well aligned with \(x\), and the average dilutes it among all \(2n\) of them, so the averaged similarity is roughly \(1/(2n)\) of the true one. Unlike the average, taking the max keeps the closest alignment. The exception is instructive: drag \(x'\) onto a mirror line, or to the center, and several copies merge. There, several alignments are right at once, and the average recovers part of its strength. Its opinion of how similar two points are depends on where they are relative to the mirrors.

The same contrast, for all points of the disc at once: each panel shows how similar every point is to the dot.

The base kernel knows nothing of the symmetry and shows a single bump. Both invariant kernels light up every copy of the dot, but the average lights them at a fraction of full strength, while under the max kernel every copy is exactly as similar to the dot as the dot is to itself (as it should be).

Folding the search space

We just found something interesting. Why is \(k_\mathrm{max}\) so good at capturing symmetries?

The answer is geometric, and can easily be visualized. Fold the disc along its mirror lines, like a paper fan, until all the copies of a point land on top of one another. What remains is a single wedge in which each point stands for a whole family of equivalent points. More formally, this is the quotient of the disc by the group, the space of equivalence classes, also called an orbifold. There is a natural distance function in this space: the distance between two points of the wedge is the length of the shortest path from one to any copy of the other, \(\min_{g \in G} \lVert x - gx' \rVert\).

The last option, ∞, takes every rotation of the disc. The copies of a point now form a whole circle, the wedge narrows to a single line, and the fold sends each point \(x\) to its distance from the center, \(\lVert x \rVert_2\). The orbifold is a segment, and the distance between two points is the difference of their radii.

Fold first, then draw

Now put an ordinary Gaussian process on the folded space, with the base kernel and these distances, and unfold it. The result is a Gaussian process on the disc whose covariance is exactly \(k_{\max}\)!3 The max kernel is not an ad hoc trick: it is what you get by modeling the function where it actually lives, on the space of equivalence classes, with the base kernel you would have used anyway.

The averaged kernel has a construction too. Draw a function \(h\) from the base Gaussian process on the whole disc, then average it over all its copies, \(\frac{1}{\lvert G \rvert}\sum_{g} h(gx)\). The result is invariant, and its covariance is exactly \(k_{\mathrm{avg}}\); it is also what you obtain by conditioning \(h\) on being invariant to \(G\).4 Both routes can start from the same random draw. Here they are, side by side.

Same draw, two invariant functions. Folding keeps \(h\) intact on every copy of the wedge: the result looks like an ordinary draw from the base prior, repeated by the symmetry. Averaging washes \(h\) out, because \(\lvert G \rvert\) unrelated values mostly cancel, except near the mirrors and the center, where some copies coincide. The averaged prior is not only fainter, it is uneven: it expects the function to vary much more near the symmetry axes than anywhere else, for no reason other than the way the kernel was built. Formally, the Gaussian process built with the average kernel is not stationary. Conversely, the Gaussian process built from \(k_\max\) is a vanilla stationary process in the wedge, which the mirrors copy across the whole disc.

A race

Time to see the kernels at work. Below, three optimizers chase the peak of the same symmetric landscape from the same five random starting points, using the upper-confidence rule from above. They differ only in their kernel. Each panel shows what the model currently believes, its posterior mean, along with every point it has evaluated; faint circles mark the true peaks. The chart tracks the cumulative regret \(R_T = \sum_{i = 1}^T (f(x^*) - f(x_i))\), the total optimization error of all evaluations so far with respect to the maximum of \(f\).

Run it a few times. With four mirrors, both invariant kernels leave the base kernel far behind and stay fairly close. With eight mirrors, \(\lvert G \rvert = 16\), the gap opens. To fit the data, the averaged model inflates its signal variance, to about five times that of the max model, and its uncertainty is then largest where copies merge: on the mirrors and at the center. That is where it spends its evaluations, more than half of them against a fifth for the max kernel.

Coda: when the max is not a kernel

Everything above relied on folding: mirror lines fold the disc flat into a wedge, and all rotations together collapse it onto a segment. Unfortunately, some groups cannot be folded that way. Take the four rotations by multiples of 90°, without mirrors. A quarter of the disc contains one copy of every point, but its two straight edges are copies of each other according to \(G\), and to measure distances between orbits they must be glued together.

A cone cannot be laid flat without tearing or stretching, so no fold turns orbit distances into ordinary distances, and \(k_{\max}\) indeed fails to be positive semi-definite here. A Gaussian process cannot use it as it is.

The fix is pragmatic. Given the points \(D\) evaluated so far, form the matrix \(K = k_{\max}(D, D)\), set its negative eigenvalues to zero to obtain \(K_+\), and extend it to new points with the Nyström formula

\[k_+(x, x') = k_{\max}(x, D)\, K_+^{\dagger}\, k_{\max}(D, x').\]

The result is a valid invariant kernel that agrees with \(k_{\max}\) on \(D\) whenever \(K\) was already positive semi-definite, at the same asymptotic cost per iteration as the averaged kernel. Here are the two kernels side by side. Drag the reference point \(x_0\), change the number of data points, or switch groups.

With rotations by 90°, about a third of the eigenvalues of \(K\) are negative and set to zero. The two kernels then differ by a few hundredths, even at the data points, and the gap shrinks only slowly as data accumulate: it comes from the negative part of \(k_{\max}\) itself, not from a lack of data. Add the mirrors and nothing is clipped: once the data cover the disc, \(k_+\) and \(k_{\max}\) coincide.

This is the off-the-shelf version of the \(k_\max\) we propose in our paper, and our benchmarks show its advantage over the averaged kernel, which grows with the size of the group.

If you are eager for more technical details, the paper is on OpenReview, and the code is on GitHub.

Thanks for reading, and see you on the next note!

  1. D. Ginsbourger, X. Bay, O. Roustant and L. Carraro, Argumentwise invariant kernels for the approximation of invariant functions, Annales de la Faculté des Sciences de Toulouse, 2012. ↩

  2. R. Kondor, Group theoretical methods in machine learning, PhD thesis, Columbia University, 2008; T. Brown, A. Cioba and I. Bogunovic, Sample-efficient Bayesian optimisation using known invariances, NeurIPS 2024. ↩

  3. Proposition 1 in the paper. It requires a folding map that turns the distance between orbits into an ordinary Euclidean distance: folding along mirrors provides one, and so does \(x \mapsto \lVert x \rVert\) for all rotations. ↩

  4. Brown, Cioba and Bogunovic (2024), for a base kernel that is unchanged when both of its arguments are transformed together, as the Gaussian kernel is under rotations and reflections. ↩
entry.summary: When a function has symmetries, every observation yields information about multiple locations in the search space. How to tell a Bayesian optimizer about it?

entry.title: On learned ignorance
entry.content:
In late November 1437, a convoy of Venetian galleys left Constantinople for Venice carrying the Byzantine emperor, the patriarch, and a delegation sent to bring them to a council meant to reunite the Eastern and Western churches. Among the delegates was a German canon lawyer in his mid-thirties, Nicholas of Cusa. Two years later, he wrote that the central idea of his most famous book had come to him during that crossing, as what he believed was a gift from above.1

A lawyer with a taste for mathematics

Nicholas was born in 1401 in Kues, a village on the Moselle. He studied at Heidelberg, then at Padua, where he received a doctorate in canon law in 1423. In Padua he also encountered the latest work in mathematics and astronomy.

He made his name at the Council of Basel in the 1430s with a treatise on church reform, De concordantia catholica, before joining the papal side and the mission to Constantinople.

The book

De docta ignorantia, usually translated On Learned Ignorance, was finished at Kues in 1440. It has three parts: the first on God, the second on the universe, the third on Christ. Its starting point is a claim about knowledge. We come to know something by comparing it with what we already know, through proportion and measure. A finite mind can always grasp the truth more precisely, and never exactly. To know this, and to know it well, is what Cusa calls learned ignorance: the more a person knows that they do not know, he writes, the more learned they are.

As he does throughout the book, he makes the point with geometry. The intellect attempts to grasp the truth as a polygon inscribed in a circle attempts to grasp the circle: the more sides it has, the more it resembles the circle, but no finite number of sides makes it equal to the circle2 since, for a regular polygon with \(n\) sides, the covered fraction of the disc is

\[\frac{A_n}{A_\circ} \;=\; \frac{n}{2\pi}\,\sin\frac{2\pi}{n}.\]

The same habit of thought runs through the rest of the book. As a circle grows without bound, its circumference becomes indistinguishable from a straight line, and in the infinite, Cusa argues, opposites such as the curved and the straight, or the maximum and the minimum, coincide. The second book draws a startling conclusion for 1440: the universe has neither a fixed center nor a fixed boundary, and the Earth is neither its center nor at rest. It is a philosophical argument, not an astronomical model, but it came a century before Copernicus.

After the book

Cusa became a cardinal in 1448 and bishop of Brixen, in the Tyrol, in 1450. That same year he wrote a series of dialogues featuring a layman, the Idiota. One of them, De staticis experimentis, argues that nature is best known by weighing: the blood and urine of the sick and the healthy, a seed and the plant it grows into, a ball of wool before and after it takes up moisture from the air. It is one of the few works in which he appeals to experiment.In De mente, written the same year, Cusa suggests that mens, mind, takes its name from mensurare, to measure.

Exact squaring was only proved impossible in 1882, when Lindemann showed that π is transcendental.

He also returned again and again to squaring the circle, in treatises that his younger contemporary Regiomontanus took apart. He died in Todi, in Umbria, in 1464. The hospice he founded in Kues still stands, and still houses his library.

Why the name

This blog is about learning under uncertainty: how algorithms should act when they know only part of what they need, and how much they can learn from a limited number of observations. Cusa’s title names that subject better than anything I could come up with, so I borrowed it. Expect notes on my research and on ideas I find interesting, most of them with figures you can play with.

  1. In the dedicatory letter to Cardinal Giuliano Cesarini that closes the book. ↩

  2. The image itself was not new. Seventeen centuries earlier, Archimedes had squeezed the circle between inscribed and circumscribed polygons to bound \(\pi\). ↩
entry.summary: A short history of the fifteenth-century book that gave this blog its name.
